skill_title: Solve titration calculations and select indicators
notes: 20 items: 8 lifted, 12 fresh. Titration stoichiometry (c·V·n), equivalence-point pH, indicator selection.

items.question: What is the term for a solution of known concentration used in a titration?
items.explanation: Standard solution: known concentration, prepared from a primary standard. Used as the titrant.
options: A standard solution.
The analyte.
The indicator.

items.question: 2.0 g of NaOH is dissolved in 250 cm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration of the NaOH solution. (M(NaOH) = 40 g/mol.)
23.64 cm³ of 0.11 mol·dm⁻³ acid HₓY neutralises 20 cm³ of 0.26 mol·dm⁻³ NaOH. Calculate the value of x in HₓY (i.e. number of ionisable H⁺ per acid molecule).
items.explanation: n(HₓY) = 0.11 × 0.02364 = 2.6 × 10⁻³ mol. n(NaOH) = 0.26 × 0.020 = 5.2 × 10⁻³ mol. Ratio n(NaOH)/n(HₓY) = 5.2/2.6 = 2 ⇒ x = 2 (the acid is DIPROTIC).

items.question: Na₂CO₃ (0.10 mol·dm⁻³, 25.0 cm³) is titrated with HCl. The end point is reached at 28.5 cm³ of HCl. Calculate the concentration of HCl. (Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + H₂O + CO₂.)
items.explanation: n(Na₂CO₃) = 0.10 × 0.025 = 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol. From stoichiometry: n(HCl) = 2 × n(Na₂CO₃) = 5.0 × 10⁻³ mol. c(HCl) = n/V = 5.0 × 10⁻³ / 0.0285 ≈ 0.175 mol·dm⁻³.

items.question: Which INDICATOR would be BEST for a titration of Na₂CO₃ (weak base) with HCl (strong acid)? Explain.
items.expectedAnswer: Methyl orange — the equivalence point of a strong acid + weak base is below pH 7.
items.explanation: Strong acid + weak base titration: equiv pH < 7 ⇒ methyl orange (3.1–4.4) is suitable. Phenolphthalein (8.3–10) would not work.
options: Phenolphthalein, because the equivalence point is above 7.
Methyl orange — the equivalence point of a strong acid + weak base is below pH 7.
Litmus, because it works for all titrations.

items.question: Which INDICATOR is suitable for a STRONG ACID + STRONG BASE titration (equivalence pH ≈ 7)?
items.expectedAnswer: Either methyl orange or phenolphthalein — the pH jump near the equivalence point is sharp.
items.explanation: Strong-strong titration: vertical pH jump straddles 7 widely; many indicators work. Best: bromothymol blue at 6-7.6.
options: Only methyl orange works.
Neither works; no indicator can be used at pH 7.
Either methyl orange or phenolphthalein — the pH jump near the equivalence point is sharp.

items.question: Which INDICATOR is suitable for a WEAK ACID + STRONG BASE titration?
items.expectedAnswer: Phenolphthalein — the equivalence point of a weak acid + strong base is above pH 7.
items.explanation: Weak acid + strong base: equivalence pH > 7 (basic salt) ⇒ phenolphthalein matches.
options: Phenolphthalein — the equivalence point of a weak acid + strong base is above pH 7.
Methyl orange, because the equivalence point is below 7.
Any indicator works equally well.

items.question: 10.0 g of Na₂CO₃ is dissolved in 0.7 dm³ of solution. Calculate the concentration. (M(Na₂CO₃) = 106 g/mol.)
Is the pH of an Na₂CO₃ solution GREATER THAN or LESS THAN 7? Explain briefly.
items.expectedAnswer: Greater than 7 — CO₃²⁻ (salt of a weak acid) hydrolyses to give OH⁻.
items.explanation: Salt hydrolysis. Strong-base + weak-acid salt ⇒ basic solution.
options: Less than 7 — Na₂CO₃ is acidic.
Greater than 7 — CO₃²⁻ (salt of a weak acid) hydrolyses to give OH⁻.
Exactly 7 — all salts are neutral.

items.question: 150 cm³ of NaOH (unknown concentration) is added to 200 cm³ of 0.03 mol·dm⁻³ HCl. The final solution has pH = 2 ([H⁺] = 0.01 mol·dm⁻³). Calculate the initial concentration of the NaOH.
items.explanation: n(HCl) initial = 0.03 × 0.200 = 6.0 × 10⁻³ mol. Final volume = 0.150 + 0.200 = 0.350 dm³. Final n(H⁺) = 0.01 × 0.350 = 3.5 × 10⁻³ mol (excess HCl). Reacted HCl = 6.0×10⁻³ − 3.5×10⁻³ = 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol. NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O (1:1), so n(NaOH) = 2.5 × 10⁻³ mol. c(NaOH) = 2.5×10⁻³ / 0.150 ≈ 0.0167 mol·dm⁻³.

items.question: A cleaning product (ChemClean) contains ammonia (NH₃). A 20 cm³ sample is titrated with 0.175 mol·dm⁻³ HCl. Titre = 28.5 cm³. Calculate the mass of NH₃ in 1 dm³ of ChemClean. (NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl; M(NH₃) = 17 g/mol.)
items.explanation: n(HCl) = 0.175 × 0.0285 ≈ 4.99 × 10⁻³ mol. From 1:1 stoichiometry, n(NH₃) in 20 cm³ = 4.99 × 10⁻³ mol. [NH₃] = 4.99×10⁻³ / 0.020 = 0.2494 mol·dm⁻³. Mass in 1 dm³ = 0.2494 × 17 ≈ 4.24 g.

items.question: Continuing: what is the pH at the END POINT of an NH₃ + HCl titration? Justify.
items.expectedAnswer: Less than 7 — NH₄Cl is acidic (NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of a weak base).
items.explanation: Strong acid + weak base equiv ⇒ acidic salt ⇒ pH < 7.
options: Greater than 7 — the salt is basic.
Exactly 7 — acid and base neutralise completely.
Less than 7 — NH₄Cl is acidic (NH₄⁺ is the conjugate acid of a weak base).

items.question: 25.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol·dm⁻³ NaOH is titrated with HCl. What volume of 0.15 mol·dm⁻³ HCl is needed to reach the equivalence point?
What is the difference between the END POINT and the EQUIVALENCE POINT in a titration?
items.expectedAnswer: Equivalence point = stoichiometrically equal amounts mixed; end point = where the indicator changes colour.
items.explanation: Equivalence = stoichiometric. End point = observed (indicator). Choose indicator so they match.
options: Equivalence point = stoichiometrically equal amounts mixed; end point = where the indicator changes colour.
They are the same thing.
End point = stoichiometric equality; equivalence = the colour change.

items.question: Calculate the mass of NaOH needed to neutralise 50.0 cm³ of 0.20 mol·dm⁻³ H₂SO₄. (M(NaOH) = 40 g/mol; H₂SO₄ + 2NaOH → Na₂SO₄ + 2H₂O.)
If water is accidentally added to the BURETTE before the HCl titrant, what effect does this have on the calculated concentration of HCl?
items.expectedAnswer: The calculated [HCl] would be too low — diluted titrant means more volume is needed.
items.explanation: Wet burette: dilutes titrant ⇒ more volume needed ⇒ apparent [HCl] is lower than actual.
options: The calculated [HCl] would be too high.
The calculated [HCl] would be too low — diluted titrant means more volume is needed.
No effect — the burette is meant to hold water.

items.question: 1.5 g of impure CaCO₃ is reacted with 200 cm³ of 0.15 mol·dm⁻³ HCl (excess). Final pH = 1.61 (200 cm³ total volume). Calculate the mass of CaCO₃ in the sample. (CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + H₂O + CO₂; M(CaCO₃) = 100 g/mol.)
A learner uses a wet conical flask (rinsed with water but not dried) for the analyte in a titration. Does this affect the titration result?
items.expectedAnswer: No — the moles of analyte are unchanged; rinsing the flask with water doesn't affect the result.
items.explanation: Wet conical flask: dilutes analyte but moles unchanged. End point determined by moles of analyte, not its volume in the flask.
options: Yes — it dilutes the analyte and lowers the result.
Yes — the water reacts with the analyte.
No — the moles of analyte are unchanged; rinsing the flask with water doesn't affect the result.

items.question: 30.0 cm³ of a 0.15 mol·dm⁻³ HNO₃ solution is mixed with 30.0 cm³ of 0.10 mol·dm⁻³ NaOH. Calculate the pH of the final solution.
What does each piece of laboratory glassware do in a titration: (a) pipette; (b) burette; (c) conical (Erlenmeyer) flask?
items.expectedAnswer: Pipette: delivers a fixed volume of analyte; burette: delivers the titrant; conical flask: holds the analyte + indicator.
items.explanation: Pipette → analyte (fixed). Burette → titrant (variable). Conical flask → mixing site.
options: Pipette: delivers a fixed volume of analyte; burette: delivers the titrant; conical flask: holds the analyte + indicator.
Pipette holds the titrant; burette delivers the analyte; flask measures pH.
All three measure the same fixed volume.

_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_POLYPROTIC_NEUTRALISATION: Doesn't account for polyprotic acid in neutralisation
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_INDICATOR_SELECTION: Wrong indicator for the titration type
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_EQUIV_POINT_PH: Misjudges pH at equivalence point for different combinations
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_NEUTRALISATION_EXCESS: Wrong handling of excess acid or base
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_SALT_HYDROLYSIS_PH: Wrong pH for salt of strong base + weak acid (or similar)
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_TITRATION_MOLES: Wrong calculation of moles from titre and concentration
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_ENDPOINT_VS_EQUIV: Confuses end point with equivalence point
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_BURETTE_WATER_EFFECT: Wrong reasoning about water in burette
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_TITRATION_ERROR: Wrong reasoning about experimental error sources
_error_signal_vocabulary.ERR_FLASK_WATER_EFFECT: Wrong reasoning about water in conical flask
